newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Impoverished Bulgaria votes in presidential poll.
newsitem.headline: Impoverished Bulgaria votes in presidential poll.

text.p: Looming food and fuel shortages threaten to turn Sunday's presidential election in Bulgaria into a crucial mid-term test for the ex-communist government
An electorate more concerned with rising prices and the coming hardships of winter looks set to rebuff the ruling socialist party.
Many people in what is widely seen as the shakiest of the ex-Warsaw Pact east European economies say they will not vote at all.
The president's duties are largely ceremonial but the vote will provide a snapshot of the electoral mood and may prove deeply embarrassing for Prime Minister Zhan Videnov.

Several analysts believe a poor showing for the socialists could widen divisions within their ranks and may even prompt a cabinet reshuffle, though few believe their superiority in parliament will be immediately threatened.

Outgoing opposition President Zhelyu Zhelev, who is not standing for re-election, urged Bulgarians on Saturday to make the effort to vote, saying a low turnout would mean the new head of state would lack the strong mandate he needs.
"Together with his limited powers, that raises the risk of a weak president who will not fully assist in overcoming the crisis," he said in a radio broadcast.
"We should all use our right to vote so we can say that we have contributed to the future of this country."
Polls open at 6 a.m. (0400 GMT) and close at 7 p.m. (1900 GMT). Preliminary results are expected early on Monday.
A total of 13 candidates are standing. If no one wins more than half the votes, or if turnout is below 50 percent, a second round will be held next Sunday.
Videnov appeared on television on Friday night to defend his government's record and urge the 6.75 million voters to support the socialist candidate, Culture Minister Ivan Marazov.
"The opposition parties will bring nothing but chaos and destabilisation which will be fatal for economic reform and everybody's lives," he said.

Polls show Petar Stoyanov, candidate of a united opposition led by the Union of Democratic Forces, ahead of Marazov. The 44-year-old lawyer has said a big opposition win would represent a vote of no confidence in the socialists.
The Balkan country is in the grip of a severe economic crisis and a poverty spiral which has robbed many people of their faith in the political system.

While most of its former Warsaw Pact allies have seen some benefits from economic reform and are pressing for inclusion in NATO and the European Union, Bulgaria remains mired in the legacy of its communist past.
It has the lowest level of foreign investment of any country in the region and a quarter of its numerous and insolvent banks are in receivership.

The central bank is rapidly running out of money to prop up the lev and buy fuel and wheat. Its foreign exchange reserves have plunged to about $505 million from about $1.5 billion over the past year.
